questions.question: If you must brake and swerve to avoid a hazard, you should:

options.text: Brake first then swerve, or swerve first then brake.
Brake and swerve at the same time.
Choose to either brake or swerve, but not both.
Do not swerve. Only use the front brake to stop.

questions.correctAnswerText: Brake first then swerve, or swerve first then brake.
questions.explanation: If you need to brake and swerve to avoid a hazard, do these actions one at a time. Do not brake while swerving because this may cause your motorcycle to tip over.

questions.question: If a dog is chasing your motorcycle, you should:

options.text: Kick the dog away.
Ride next to the dog.
Stop and wait for the dog to lose interest.
Slow down and approach the dog, then speed up quickly.

questions.correctAnswerText: Slow down and approach the dog, then speed up quickly.
questions.explanation: If a dog is chasing you, shift down and approach it slowly. Then speed up and leave it behind. If a larger animal is in your path, brake and be ready to stop.

questions.question: Your lane position should not:

options.text: Increase your ability to see.
Keep you out of other drivers' blind spots.
Invite other drivers to share your lane.
Give you an escape route.

questions.correctAnswerText: Invite other drivers to share your lane.
questions.explanation: A good lane position should help you see better and be seen by others. It should help you avoid wind blasts, other drivers' blind spots, and road hazards. Your lane position should discourage other drivers from sharing your lane and give you a way to escape if danger appears.

questions.question: Because other drivers have trouble seeing motorcycles at night, riders should:

options.text: Ride slower at night.
Use the horn repeatedly at night.
Not ride at night.
Stay directly in front of another vehicle so their headlights shine on you.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride slower at night.
questions.explanation: To ride safely at night, ride slower, increase your following distance, use the headlights of the car ahead to see farther, use your high beam (unless you are behind or facing another vehicle), and be ready to adjust your lane position.

questions.question: Face shields and goggles:

options.text: Will probably never need to be replaced.
Get scratched and become weak over time, so replace them regularly.
Should be made of material that breaks easily so they break away during a crash.
Should block all air from passing through.

questions.correctAnswerText: Get scratched and become weak over time, so replace them regularly.
questions.explanation: Face shields and goggles are made of plastic and will get scratched and become brittle as time passes. Replace them often to keep your protection and comfort at their best.

questions.question: When crossing angled railroad tracks, the safest approach is usually to:

options.text: Go straight ahead in your lane.
Approach at a 45-degree angle.
Approach at a 90-degree angle.
Go at a fast speed.

questions.correctAnswerText: Go straight ahead in your lane.
questions.explanation: The safest way to cross angled railroad tracks is to go straight in your lane. Turning to hit the tracks at a right angle can be dangerous because it may push you into another lane.

questions.question: When braking on a slippery surface, you should:

options.text: Use both the front and rear brakes.
Use hard pressure on the front brake to prevent the front tire from locking.
Use only the rear brake.
Use only one brake at a time.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use both the front and rear brakes.
questions.explanation: On slippery surfaces, use both brakes to slow down. Squeeze the brake lever slowly to keep the front wheel from locking and use gentle pressure on the rear brake.

questions.question: If a small animal enters your lane while you are in traffic, you should:

options.text: Do whatever you can, including swerve into other lanes, to avoid the animal.
Change lanes as quickly as possible.
Stay in your lane.
Flash your lights to scare the animal away.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stay in your lane.
questions.explanation: Try to avoid hitting an animal safely. However, if you are in traffic, stay in your lane. Swerving into another lane to avoid a small animal can cause you to hit another vehicle. Hitting a small animal is safer than hitting another car.

questions.question: When riding in a group, less experienced riders should position themselves:

options.text: Just behind the leader.
In front of the group.
At the back of the group.
Beside the leader.

questions.correctAnswerText: Just behind the leader.
questions.explanation: Less experienced riders should ride toward the front of the group, just behind the leader. This lets experienced riders watch over them without forcing the less experienced rider to lead the group.

questions.question: Because motorcycles are small, they seem to be:

options.text: Going faster than they really are.
Going slower than they really are.
Stopped when they are actually moving.
Closer than they really are.

questions.correctAnswerText: Going faster than they really are.
questions.explanation: Because of their small size, motorcycles often appear to be traveling faster than they actually are.

questions.question: What formation should a group of riders use when entering a curve?

options.text: Pyramid
Staggered
Single-file
Compressed

questions.correctAnswerText: Single-file
questions.explanation: Use a staggered formation when riding normally. But use single-file when taking curves, turning, or entering or exiting a highway.

questions.question: As weight moves to the front of your bike while braking, you should:

options.text: Gradually increase pressure to the front brake.
Use more rear brake pressure.
Not worry. The weight transfer will not affect your motorcycle.
Try to lock the front tire.

questions.correctAnswerText: Gradually increase pressure to the front brake.
questions.explanation: As you brake, gradually press harder on the front brake lever. The weight moves forward to the front tire, so you need more front brake pressure.

questions.question: Which statement is true?

options.text: The front and rear brakes provide equal stopping power.
The front brake provides more stopping power than the rear brake.
The rear brake provides more stopping power than the front brake.
Only the front brake should be used when braking.

questions.correctAnswerText: The front brake provides more stopping power than the rear brake.
questions.explanation: The front brake is stronger than the rear brake. It provides at least 70 percent of the total stopping power. Always use both brakes when you slow down or stop.

questions.question: When another vehicle is passing you, where should you ride in your lane?

options.text: Ride in the left portion of your lane.
Ride in the center portion of your lane.
Ride in the right portion of your lane.
Try to get onto the shoulder.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the center portion of your lane.
questions.explanation: Ride in the center of your lane when being passed. Riding on either side of the lane is dangerous. The passing driver might not see you or might return to your lane too quickly.

questions.question: When following another vehicle, is it safe to ride on the far side of your lane?

options.text: Yes, because other drivers will see you easily.
No, because drivers do not check their side mirrors often and may not see you.
Yes, because a passenger may tell the driver you are there.
No, because the law requires you to ride in the center of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: No, because drivers do not check their side mirrors often and may not see you.
questions.explanation: Most drivers check their rearview mirror more often than their side mirrors. Ride in the center of your lane so the driver in front can see you in their rearview mirror.

questions.question: What is true about the center portion of a lane?

options.text: It is always the best part of the lane for a motorcycle.
It often has oil and grease, but is usually safe for riding.
It often has oil and grease, and is never safe for riding.
It is the smoothest part of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: It often has oil and grease, but is usually safe for riding.
questions.explanation: Oil from cars collects in the center of each lane. On dry roads, this area still has enough grip for motorcycles to ride safely. Avoid large buildups of oil and grease at busy intersections or toll booths.

questions.question: Under normal conditions, what is the minimum following distance you should keep?

options.text: One second.
Two seconds.
Three seconds.
Four seconds.

questions.correctAnswerText: Four seconds.
questions.explanation: Keep at least four seconds of distance behind the vehicle in front of you. Increase this distance if conditions are poor.

questions.question: A group of riders in staggered formation is passing a car on the left. After the lead rider passes, they should:

options.text: Return to the right portion of their original lane.
Return to the center portion of their original lane.
Return to the left portion of their original lane.
Signal the other riders to follow.

questions.correctAnswerText: Return to the left portion of their original lane.
questions.explanation: Move into the left portion of your lane after passing and keep your passing speed. This creates space in front of the car for the next rider. Moving to the right side is unsafe and might cause the next rider to pass too early.

questions.question: The oily strip in the center of a lane is:

options.text: Never safe for motorcyclists.
Usually safe for motorcyclists, unless it is raining.
Should always be avoided since other parts of the lane are better.
Good for traction on most motorcycle tires.

questions.correctAnswerText: Usually safe for motorcyclists, unless it is raining.
questions.explanation: Oil from cars collects in the center of lanes. On dry roads, it still provides enough traction for safe riding. The oily strip is usually narrow, so you can ride beside it and still be in the center lane portion.

questions.question: Studies show that nearly ______ of riders killed in motorcycle crashes had been drinking.

options.text: 20 percent
40 percent
60 percent
80 percent

questions.correctAnswerText: 40 percent
questions.explanation: Alcohol causes many motorcycle crashes, especially fatal ones. About 40 percent of riders killed in motorcycle accidents had been drinking.
